Visually only: when the foam has settled down and the bubbles have gotten larger and more viscous as the mixture boils, your jelly is ready to put into jars; with more experience, you will be able to eyeball the mixture and get a sense of its viscosity
Using a cold plate: keep a plate chilling in your freezer, then splash a blob of the jelly onto the plate and wait one minute; if you can pull your finger through the blob and leave a clean path with the jelly wrinkled around it, your jelly is done
Using a thermometer: when your mixture reaches 220 degrees Fahrenheit (or 105 degress Celsius), it is ready to put into jars


Pour mixture into hot Mason jars and close with fresh snap lids and rings (refer again to Food in Jars for a good explanation)
Process in a boiling water canner for the appropriate amount of time for the size of the jars (refer to this chart from the University of Minnesota for specifics related to altitude, jar size, and other variables)


To make your own pectin: follow steps 1 through 4 above, but use cores and peels from apples (or entire underripe apples) as your base fruit.

food/research/research-on-gluten-free-fl.title: Research on gluten-free flour mixes
food/research/research-on-gluten-free-fl.content:
Forever ago, I found a chart that listed all of the readily available non-wheat flours and their properties, for the purpose of helping people bake gluten-free things more easily. I can’t find that chart, so I’m looking around for other options now, and here’s what I’ve found so far.
Between the Fork and Beans, Gluten Free Girl, and The Gluten Free Lifesaver sites, I see you can group flours into the following categories:

Starchy/light: arrowroot, cornstarch, potato atarch, tapioca (starch or flour), sweet rice (mochiko)

These generally are used to add texture and lightness to the finished product


Whole grain/medium: yellow or green pea, fava bean, chickpea, millet, oat, quinoa, sorghum, white rice, roasted soybean (kinako)

Legume flours tend to give a very good rise but have distinct bean flavours
Sorghum: gives results similar to wheat in lightness; has a nutty flavour
Millet: same protein content as wheat; powdery texture; sweet flavour
Oat: very similar result as wheat flour; check for certified non-cross-contaminated flour


Heavy: almond, amaranth, brown rice, buckwheat, coconut, cornflour, cornmeal, teff, potato flour

Coconut flour absorbs liquid much more readily than other flours, so you shouldn’t use it in a ratio higher than 25%
Potato flour: same as coconut flour
Nut flours will contribute fat to a recipe (avoid in pastry)



Gluten Free Girl recommends a blend of 40% whole grain/heavy flours to 60% starches, while Fork and Beans recommends experimenting with these ratios:

1:1 starch to whole grain

This pancake recipe from Gluten Free Baking uses a 1:1 ratio, approximately
This pie pastry recipe from Serious Eats uses about a 1:1 ratio by weight, with about 0.25 part coconut flour added for stability
This pastry flour mix from the Food Network uses a 1:1 ratio by weight almost exactly


2:1 starch to medium

This all-purpose mix from Thank Heavens uses a 2:1 ratio with a small amount of heavy for body


1:2 starch to medium
1:1:1 starch to medium to heavy

From The Gluten Free Lifesaver, I’ve grabbed their gluten free ratios cheat sheet; note that it’s by volume and not weight:

When it comes to binders like xanthan or guar gum, they should be added in the ratios recommended by the manufacturer.

tech/research/adfection-hardening-runboo.title: AdFection hardening runbook
tech/research/adfection-hardening-runboo.content:
This runbook contains steps to harden personal devices (Kubuntu, Android, Windows, macOS) against AdFection, the spyware technique documented by Citizen Lab on October 15, 2026. AdFection is a delivery technique that uses website and app advertising networks to deploy spyware (in the documented case, Candiru’s) onto target machines upon page load.
The systems the malware exploits
AdFection exploits standard online advertisement auction processes and systems. When a webpage or mobile app has an ad slot and the page containing it loads:

The app/page code running on the user’s device sends a request (bid) to an ad exchange
Advertisers automatically bid for the chance to show that user an ad
The exchange picks the winner and pushes the ad

All of this happens in under a second, hundreds of billions of times a day. Two kinds of platform sit between the parties:

Advertisers buy through a demand-side platform (DSP)
Sites and apps sell ad slots through a supply-side platform (SSP)

The bid carries data about the user so buyers can decide whether it’s worth their money to bid. Most data comes from SSP code embedded in the website the user visits or the SDK used to develop the mobile app, but some is supplied by the user’s mobile carrier itself:

















































Data typeData sourceMobile advertising IDCore function of Android and iOSDevice detailsSSP codePrecise locationSSP codeIP addressSSP codeSite/app containing the ad slotSSP codeAd slot specs (format, placement, price, restrictions, security flag, supported APIs, SDK used)SSP codeAd-firm cookie IDsAd firms’ tracking code in the browser, exchanged between firms by ID syncingPage cookiesAd’s script, reading cookies set on the page showing the adReal IP behind a VPNAd’s script, via WebRTC leakPhone numberMobile carriers’ “header enrichment”, frequently used for convenience (e.g. letting a site recognize a user by phone number to sign in automatically)
A combination of this information easily allows advertisers to target a single person. And since the winning ad can include code for the target machine to execute within the ad slot, that provides the payload delivery mechanism.
An Israeli ad firm, Discover-Tech, bought ad slots that included the ability to deploy a script. On load, the script gathered information about the client machine, then sent it to the Discover-Tech server to check it against a list of targets. Non-targets saw a normal ad, while targets got code that loaded a browser exploit that installed Candiru’s spyware. Because the malware only went to chosen devices, the networks serving the ads never saw it.
The payload found in the Al Jazeera sample machine was a Windows DLL persisting via COM hijack; this lets the malware run in a process the host system classified as legitimate.
Hardening procedure
Linux desktop (Kubuntu)

Automatic security updates: patches known bugs on the user machine; sudo apt install unattended-upgrades && sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
Block ads: removes a major distribution channel; install uBlock Origin in Firefox and keep its default filter lists on

Chrome doesn’t support full uBlock Origin, only uBlock Origin Lite (it can’t run its own filtering logic, and its main lists update only with extension updates); prefer to switch primary browsing to Firefox and use Chrome only if sites are broken


Block third-party cookies: removes one way to target a specific device

Firefox: Settings → Privacy & Security → Enhanced Tracking Protection → Strict
Chrome: Settings → Privacy and security → Third-party cookies → Block third-party cookies


Turn off JavaScript JIT: JIT speeds up page code by sacrificing security, in that browsers with it on skip interpreting every line of page code and instead convert frequently-run elements into machine code

Firefox: browse to about:config and set javascript.options.ion and javascript.options.baselinejit to false
Chrome: browse to chrome://settings/content/v8 → Don’t allow sites to use the V8 optimizer


Stop WebRTC IP leaks

Firefox, breaks browser video calls: about:config → media.peerconnection.enabled = false

This closes every WebRTC leak route at once and removes WebRTC as an attack surface
Candiru has exploited a WebRTC zero-day in Chrome before (CVE-2022-2294)
Choose this if you don’t make video calls in the browser


Firefox, keeps calls: about:config → set media.peerconnection.ice.default_address_only, media.peerconnection.ice.no_host and media.peerconnection.ice.proxy_only_if_behind_proxy to true

This limits which IP addresses WebRTC reveals, but the WebRTC code still runs and can still be attacked


Chrome, keeps calls

Install WebRTC Leak Prevent, set its IP handling policy to “Disable non-proxied UDP (force proxy)”, and tick “Allow in incognito”; OR
Set enterprise policy WebRtcIPHandling = disable_non_proxied_udp in a JSON file under /etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/
Same vulnerability as above; Chrome removed its flag for turning WebRTC off




Configure system-wide DNS filtering: block advertising domains; set a filtering DNS resolver in NetworkManager for each connection, or run a Pi-hole device on the network

Android

Automatic updates: patches known bugs on the user machine; install system updates, and update Chrome and Android System WebView from the Play Store
Delete the advertising ID: removes one way to target a specific device; Settings → Privacy → Ads → Delete advertising ID, which removes the ID without issuing a new one

Older Android versions use a different path


Configure Private DNS filtering: blocks advertising domains, including in apps; Settings → Network & internet → Private DNS → enter a filtering provider’s hostname
Turn on Advanced Protection (Android 16): turns on Android’s most effective security features; Settings → Security & privacy → Other settings → Advanced Protection → turn on Device protection

Blocks sideloading and installs from unknown sources, enables Memory Tagging Extension for supported apps, and turns off the JavaScript optimizer in Chrome


Turn off JavaScript JIT in Chrome: Advanced Protection already does this in Chrome; if you skip Advanced Protection, use Chrome → Settings → Privacy and security → Security → JavaScript optimization and security → turn off the V8 optimizer

This is a Chrome setting, so ads shown inside other apps’ web views may not be covered


Block ads and third-party cookies in a browser that supports extensions: removes a major distribution channel; install Firefox, add uBlock Origin with its default filter lists on, and set Settings → Enhanced Tracking Protection → Strict

Chrome on Android can’t run extensions, so use Firefox as the primary browser


Cut ad-funded apps: removes exposure to in-app ads; remove or pay for ad-free versions of ad-heavy apps

Apps that showed these ads include MX Player and Lark Player (over one million each) and Viber (over 700,000)



Windows and macOS
Both platforms take the same Firefox and Chrome steps as Kubuntu (uBlock Origin, third-party cookie blocking, JIT off, WebRTC leak prevention). Platform-specific steps:
Windows

Automatic updates: patches known bugs on the user machine; leave Windows Update and browser auto-update on
Turn off the advertising ID: removes one way to target a specific device; Settings → Privacy & security → General → turn off personalized ads using your advertising ID
Turn off JavaScript JIT in Edge (if you use Edge; Firefox and Chrome follow the Kubuntu steps): Edge → Settings → Privacy, search, and services → Security → Enhance your security on the web → Strict
Configure system-wide DNS filtering: blocks advertising domains, including in apps; Settings → Network & internet → your connection → DNS server assignment → a filtering resolver, encrypted if offered

macOS

Automatic updates: patches known bugs on the user machine; leave automatic updates and Background Security Improvements (the successor to Rapid Security Responses) on; check System Settings → Privacy & Security → Background Security Improvements
Turn off personalized ads: removes one way to target a specific device; System Settings → Privacy & Security → Apple Advertising → turn off Personalized Ads
Turn on Lockdown Mode: disables JIT JavaScript compilation in web browsing unless you exempt a site; System Settings → Privacy & Security → Lockdown Mode

This acts on Apple’s WebKit engine, so Firefox and Chrome need their own JIT settings


Configure system-wide DNS filtering: blocks advertising domains, including in apps; System Settings → Network → your connection → Details → DNS → a filtering resolver, encrypted if offered

Checking your work

WebRTC

Check: turn on your VPN and open BrowserLeaks WebRTC
Expected result: your real public IP doesn’t appear


Ad blocking

Check: load a news site that normally shows ads
Expected result: the uBlock icon shows a non-zero count and ad slots stay empty


DNS filtering

a. Desktop (Kubuntu, Windows, macOS)

Check: run nslookup mtrtb.com (a Discover-Tech domain)
Expected result: a filtering resolver that lists it returns 0.0.0.0 or no answer

A normal IP means your list doesn’t cover it
An error with no answer can also mean a failed lookup, so retry with a known good domain




b. Android

Check: open Settings → Network & internet → Private DNS, then load mtrtb.com in the browser
Expected result: Private DNS shows your provider’s hostname, and the page fails to load


c. Windows

Check: open Settings → Network & internet → your connection
Expected result: DNS server assignment lists your filtering resolver


d. macOS

Check: open System Settings → Network → your connection → Details → DNS
Expected result: the DNS tab lists your filtering resolver




JavaScript JIT

a. Chrome (desktop)

Check: browse to chrome://settings/content/v8
Expected result: the page lists the optimizer as disallowed


b. Firefox (desktop)

Check: browse to about:config and search for javascript.options.ion and javascript.options.baselinejit
Expected result: both read false


c. Chrome (Android)

Check: open Chrome → Settings → Privacy and security → Security → JavaScript optimization and security
Expected result: the V8 optimizer reads off


d. Edge (Windows)

Check: open Edge → Settings → Privacy, search, and services → Security
Expected result: Enhance your security on the web reads Strict




Advertising ID

a. Android

Check: open Settings → Privacy → Ads
Expected result: the screen shows no advertising ID


b. Windows

Check: open Settings → Privacy & security → General
Expected result: Personalized ads using your advertising ID reads off


c. macOS

Check: open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Apple Advertising
Expected result: Personalized Ads reads off




Platform hardening mode

a. Android Advanced Protection

Check: open Advanced Protection
Expected result: Device protection reads on


b. macOS Lockdown Mode

Check: open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Lockdown Mode
Expected result: Lockdown Mode reads on




Automatic updates (Kubuntu)

Check: run systemctl status unattended-upgrades
Expected result: the service reports active



Gaps left after all that work
You’ve just made it more expensive and complicated for an attack to land on your device, but your devices still aren’t bulletproof.

Zero-day exploits still work: only if a bug is already known can an update patch it; while turning off JIT narrows the attack surface, it’s not closed since recent Chrome builds can still run WebAssembly with the V8 optimizer disallowed, depending on version and platform
Blocklists lag behind the reality of the rotating infrastructure used by attackers: Discover-Tech moved between many domains and also used CloudFront distributions; no one can decisively block a not-previously-known domain, and pre-emptively blocking shared CDN hostnames will also break legitimate sites
Browser controls don’t touch in-app ads: in this case, most ad bids were embedded in mobile apps

Also complicating things: if an app uses its own encrypted DNS, this bypasses system DNS filtering


Removing advertising IDs still leaves IP targeting possible: attackers can target a device by IP address alone, and home IP addresses tend to be persistent and stable. Worse, ads served to non-targets still sent device data back to Discover-Tech, including the public IPv6 address
Mobile carriers leak phone numbers via header enrichment: a different attacker used Discover-Tech infrastructure to exploit header enrichment, mapping advertising IDs to carrier-issued phone numbers (this relies on plain HTTP requests); no step above stops this, and the only user-side mitigation is avoiding plain HTTP (for example with HTTPS-only mode) or using Wi-Fi instead of cellular
Attacker can still deliver exploit via non-ad means: the Candiru attack has also succeeded via a compromised news website, not via ads; the ad-specific steps (ad blocking, DNS filtering, advertising-ID removal) don’t defend against this or against zero-click malware delivered via messengers; only the general steps (updates, JIT off, Lockdown Mode, Advanced Protection) still help
Attacker can still build a profile without ads: Discover-Tech’s ID syncing typically happened during website visits even when the user never received a Discover-Tech ad
Users can’t detect infection: Al Jazeera used network logs to confirm infections; users have almost no reliable way to tell an infection has happened

tech/research/trinity-college-dublin-stu.title: Trinity College Dublin study on Google Messages and Dialer emitting tracking metadata
tech/research/trinity-college-dublin-stu.content:
A 2022 Trinity College Dublin study (PDF; news release) found Google’s Messages and Phone apps sent a log to Google of every text made/received (including the timestamp and a truncated content hash) and every call made (time and duration).
Affected workflows
This assumes both parties are using the Google Dialer and Messages apps.
Phone call

Alice calls Bob on the cellular network
Alice’s phone logs the call setup events (dialpad opened, each digit typed, call connecting)
Bob’s phone logs the incoming call event
Alice and Bob end the call
Alice’s phone sends the call’s duration to Google over the data network
Bob’s phone sends the call’s duration to Google over the data network
Both phones send a notification to Google Analytics over the data network that a call happened, each with the phone’s advertising ID

Google could use the nearly identical call-duration values to infer that the two numbers were in the same phone call. This was even worse with default settings; if the receiving phone has “Caller ID & Spam Protection” on, it straight-up reported the caller’s number to Google.
The app didn’t disclose this in its privacy policy or provide a way to opt out.
SMS message

Alice texts Bob using her Android Messages app
Alice’s Messages app sends a fingerprint of the message (a hash of the message text and the hour it was sent) to Google’s Clearcut logging service, tagged with her Android ID
Bob receives Alice’s text message over the cellular network
Bob’s Messages app computes the same hash and sends it to Google over the data network
Bob’s Messages app reports Alice’s phone number to Google over the data network
Both phones report to Google Analytics over the data network that a message was sent/received at a specific time, each with the phone’s advertising ID

Assuming Bob was using Google Messages, Google’s server saw two matching hash values from two different device IDs, which could confirm their devices were in communication with each other.
Evidence
Google Messages



























































Field / stringWhere it appearsExample value seen in the studyWhat it  provessha256HashMsgClearcut logger: the ANDROID_MESSAGING log on the sending phone has a BUGLE_MESSAGE  event with SENT status"247836537599431109"Nothing by itselfsha256HashMsgClearcut logger: the ANDROID_MESSAGING log on the receiving phone has a BUGLE_MESSAGE event with  RECEIVED status"247836537599431109" (same as above)Two devices were involved in the exchange of a message with the exact same contents during the same clock hoursha256HashPrevMsgBoth of the rows above"200428458475182371" (matches on both ends too)The fingerprint of the previous message in the conversation, also matching on both phones — reinforces that this is designed to chain and link an entire conversation, not just one message.incomingPhoneNumberClearcut logger, CARRIER_SERVICES log source, receiving phone only"+353872...351"The receiving phone directly reports the sender’s real phone number to Google. This is a separate, more blunt disclosure than the fingerprint — an actual phone number, not a scrambled code.google_ad_idGoogle/Firebase Analytics, both phones, event ACTIVE_EVENT"916c714a-e838-479d-a7a6-3325d838da5f"This is the phone’s Google advertising ID — the same identifier Google uses to target ads. Attaching it to a “you just texted someone” event is what lets this data plug into the rest of your ad profile.firebase_instance_idSame Analytics event"eVpvvohEDCqhfIGC7pXLnv"A per-app-install ID that the paper shows is linked back to the phone’s permanent Android ID — i.e., not anonymous or resettable in practice.(tagged at the message-batch level, not a field inside each event)All Clearcut (not Analytics) eventshandset Android IDThe paper shows this ID is separately linkable to the SIM card serial number, the phone’s hardware serial number, and the Google account signed into the phone — so “just a device ID” still traces back to a real person."E2EChatIntegrityMetricsHelperImpl"Decompiled app code (not a network event — found inside the app itself)—The internal programmer-facing label Google gave to the code that builds the fingerprint. “E2E” commonly means “end-to-end” — the researchers read this as confirming the fingerprint’s real purpose is linking both ends of a conversation, not just debugging.
Why a rainbow table of sorts could actually be built
The hash uses the hour a message was sent as an input, which means that the exact same message sent at 11:59 and at 12:00 would have different hash values. This means that, while it’s not simple and straightforward to build a durable rainbow table,
What Google said and did

Google’s stated reason for the fingerprint: detecting bugs where messages arrive out of order (“message sequencing bugs”).
Google committed to stop collecting the message fingerprint starting with Messages app version 10.9.160 (an unspecified later version was promised to also drop the sender’s phone number and the SIM card ID collection — no version number given for those two).
Google told journalists the data was “not — and were never — used for targeting ads” and was covered by “strict internal access controls.” The paper only shows what leaves the phone and how it’s tagged; it has no visibility into Google’s servers, so it can’t confirm or refute that claim either way.


Google Dialer
The evidence: exact strings, and what each one proves















































Field / stringWhere it appearsExample value seen in the studyWhat it actually provescallDurationClearcut logger- ANDROID_DIALER log source- calling phone- event USER_PARTICIPATED_IN_A_CALL12344 (milliseconds → 12.344s)The length of the call the caller’s phone reports to Google.callDurationClearcut logger- ANDROID_DIALER log source- receiving phone- event USER_PARTICIPATED_IN_A_CALL12865 (12.865s)The receiving phone’s own independently-logged duration for the same call — close but not identical to the caller’s value. The ~0.5s gap is attributed to normal network delay between one phone hanging up and the other being told. This near-match (not an exact cryptographic match, unlike texts) is what lets Google probabilistically pair the two phones.searchQuery- queryLength: 1 through queryLength: 10Clearcut logger- ANDROID_DIALER log source- calling phone—Each individual keypress while dialing is logged with its own timestamp — i.e. Google receives a keystroke-by-keystroke timing trace of you typing the phone number, not just the final number.incomingPhoneNumberClearcut logger- SCOOBY_EVENTS log source (Caller ID & Spam Protection, on by default)- receiving phone"+353872...351"The direct phone number of the person calling you, sent to Google. The paper states this fires “every time a call is received and even if the phone number is in the handset contacts database.”google_ad_id- firebase_instance_idGoogle/Firebase Analytics- calling phone, event OUTGOING_CALL_PLACED- receiving phone, event INCOMING_CALL_RECEIVED"916c714a-e838-479d-a7a6-3325d838da5f"Same mechanism as texts: ties the fact that a call happened to the phone’s advertising identity.Android IDAll Clearcut (not Analytics) events, per Table IV in the paper- tagged at the message-batch level—Same identity-linkage point as Messages — the interaction log (dialpad opens, call history views, contact searches) is tied to a durable, traceable device ID, not an anonymous session.
A genuine discrepancy worth flagging
The paper’s own measurement says the caller-ID number report fires on every incoming call, even for contacts already saved on your phone. But per the paper’s “Response From Google” section, Google told the researchers the spam-protection data collection “only occurs for phone numbers not in the handset contacts list.” Those two statements directly conflict — either Google’s explanation to the researchers was inaccurate, or the behavior differs from what the researchers measured. The paper doesn’t resolve this; it just reports both, side by side. Worth naming directly if you cite this, rather than picking whichever side is more convenient.
What Google said and did (Dialer-specific)

Google’s stated purpose for the Caller ID/Spam Protection number collection: user protection from spam calls.
Google committed to fuzz the SCOOBY_EVENTS timestamp to the nearest hour, server-side immediately and client-side from Dialer app version v75 onwards — this is a real, version-numbered commitment, unlike the Messages phone-number/ICCID fixes. Note this only coarsens the timestamp; it doesn’t stop the phone number itself from being sent.
Google committed to remove call-related event logging from Firebase Analytics for both Dialer and Messages, again with no version number given.
Google planned a “product tour” and a visual in-app indicator to tell users Caller ID/Spam Protection is on and how to disable it — an acknowledgment that most users likely don’t know it’s active, since it’s on by default.

The paper says Google’s stated justification for the hashing was to detect message sequencing bugs. However, there are some problems with this as an explanation:

Google never allowed users to consent to or opt out of this behaviour; a legitimate, value-added service would do so
There’s no user-supporting reason why data that can be linked to your hardware ID, SIM ICCID, and Google Account, need to be sent out to a logging service

Conclusions
Per the paper, Google committed to stop collecting the hash in Messages v10.9.160, and the phone number and SIM ICCID in later, unspecified releases. If it were a clean value-add to users, it would make more sense to just keep and disclose the functionality; this comes across more like Google sullenly withdrawing their hand from the cookie jar once called out.
Tech learnings
Inspecting traffic
The researchers used  mitmproxy 6.0.2 on their Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point to capture traffic. They used an iptables rule to redirect HTTP/S traffic to port 8080 (the mitmproxy listener).
They specifically blocked UDP on 443 to force traffic using the proprietary QUIC protocol (TL;DR) to fail over to TCP.
Related questions
Did Google ever remove the phone and SIM ICCID logging?
Unverified from the web searching I’ve done so far.
Does Google normally announce updates to issues like this anywhere?
TL;DR: not in detail or proactively.
The Play Store has generic release notes, but they’re too vague to pin a specific bugfix to a specific version, and official blogs (Android Developers Blog, Google Security Blog, Google’s “Safety Center”) usually concern security patches (CVEs), major feature launches, or policy changes Google wants credit for; a privacy-violating “oopsie” doesn’t fit that brand.
In this case, Google privately responded to Leith during co-ordinated vulnerability disclosure, which he chose to publish in his own paper. Google also provided damage-control statements to journalists (The Register, Android Police, MobileSyrup) once the story broke in March 2022. These were not proactive public statements.
How would I verify the status of this vulnerability myself?
Follow Leith’s methodology in the paper: decompile sequential Messages APKs from spring 2022 onward and note which version’s code no longer has  CARRIER_SERVICES logging phone numbers and collecting SIM ICCIDs.

tech/tinkering/blog-architecture.title: An overview of this blog's architecture
tech/tinkering/blog-architecture.content:
I have a dedicated Obsidian vault as the authoritative source for site content, and this vault is remotely accessible via the Obsidian Sync service. I chose Obsidian because I’m already familiar with its use and it’s an easy, low-barrier-to-entry WYSIWYG editor available on multiple platforms.
Because plain Markdown has its limits when it comes to visual appeal, I opted for a separate tool to transform it into a static site. I chose Quartz 5 for no particular reason other than that it showed up early in my searching and seemed feature-rich and user-friendly enough for my purposes.
A Bash script builds, commits, and pushes the site code to a GitHub repo, where GitHub Pages serves it.
Usage
The system supports this user workflow to update the blog:

In Obsidian, create a note with QuickAdd (New journal entry or New recipe), which:

Fills in the frontmatter via Templater; and
Drops the file, unpublished, into the vault root


Proceed to write the entry
Run the Publish note command, which flips publish to true
In the staging repo, run publish.sh

Important file locations
Content source
A single Obsidian vault is the authoritative source of all content published to the blog. The vault can reside anywhere on the filesystem as long as the tools called by the publish.sh script can access the path.
The vault has its own git repo, separate from the staging and live site repos, committed periodically by a cron job (~/bin/vault-autocommit.sh). created/modified frontmatter is user-edited; use git log --follow on a file for an actual audit trail.
Staging repo
This is a local repo that contains the Quartz installation files and its build artifacts, as well as publish.sh. It must contain a symlink to the Obsidian vault and be able to access the local clone of the live site repo.
Live site repo
This is a local clone of the GitHub repo that hosts the live site’s source code. The final steps of publish.sh copy the artifacts from the staging repo to the live site repo, then commit the changes to main and push to the remote, which updates the live site.
Note management helpers
The vault’s tools/ folder (not published) holds templates and scripts supporting note creation and publishing. They use the Templater and QuickAdd community plugins.
tools/journal-entry.md and tools/recipe.md are Templater templates that QuickAdd’s New journal entry and New recipe commands fill in on creation. The new file is placed at the vault root and the user is expected to file it into the appropriate directory.
tools/publish-note.js is a QuickAdd user script that is invoked as the Publish note Obsidian command. When your active note is ready to publish, run the command; this sets publish: true. It works on any note in the vault except tools/ itself. The note stays where it was written, and created/modified stay whatever the author set.
Stages
Build
Quartz builds a static site as follows:

Parses the vault Markdown files and Obsidian-specific syntax
Applies transformations per the plugins in quartz.config.yaml
Renders the result to HTML using Preact components
Writes the finished files into public/

Publish
publish.sh is a script that runs in the staging repo. Its job is to validate the build environment and output, transform the contents of the source Obsidian vault into website source code, copy outputs to the live repo, and commit/push to the remote as follows:

Check $LIVE_REPO_PATH is a valid git clone
Confirm $CONTENT_DIR resolves to the vault path
Run the Quartz build and confirms it produced public/index.html
Write .nojekyll directly into public/
Confirm public/ holds no stray .md files
Sync public/ into the live site repo with rsync -a --delete
Commits and pushes from the live site repo


publish.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Builds the Quartz site locally and publishes the rendered output.
#
# You must first set VAULT_PATH, STAGING_REPO_PATH, LIVE_REPO_PATH,
# and CONTENT_DIR in the environment.
#
# Usage: VAULT_PATH=... STAGING_REPO_PATH=... LIVE_REPO_PATH=...
# CONTENT_DIR=... ./publish.sh [commit message]
 
set -euo pipefail
 
: "${VAULT_PATH:?set VAULT_PATH to the absolute Obsidian vault path}"
: "${STAGING_REPO_PATH:?set STAGING_REPO_PATH to this repo's path}"
: "${LIVE_REPO_PATH:?set LIVE_REPO_PATH to the live site repo's path}"
: "${CONTENT_DIR:?set CONTENT_DIR to the name of the symlink to the vault}"
MESSAGE="${1:-Publish site}"
 
cd "${STAGING_REPO_PATH}"
 
if [ ! -d "${LIVE_REPO_PATH}/.git" ]; then
  echo "error: ${LIVE_REPO_PATH} must be a clone of a git repo." >&2
  exit 1
fi
 
# CONTENT_DIR must resolve to VAULT_PATH
RESOLVED_CONTENT_DIR="$(readlink -f "${CONTENT_DIR}")"
if [ "${RESOLVED_CONTENT_DIR}" != "$(readlink -f "${VAULT_PATH}")" ]; then
  echo "error: ${STAGING_REPO_PATH}/${CONTENT_DIR} must resolve to ${VAULT_PATH}." >&2
  exit 1
fi
 
# Build first to fail faster and avoid shipping a broken site.
#
# Pass the resolved vault path, not the CONTENT_DIR symlink itself: Quartz
# globs for content with a gitignore-aware search that walks up from the
# given directory looking for .gitignore files. However, this repo's
# own .gitignore ignores the symlink to support user-configurable symlink
# names, so the resolved path needs to be passed into the build command.
 
echo "Building..."
npx quartz build -d "${RESOLVED_CONTENT_DIR}"
 
if [ ! -f "public/index.html" ]; then
  echo "error: build did not produce public/index.html; aborting." >&2
  exit 1
fi
 
# GitHub Pages runs Jekyll by default, which drops underscore-prefixed paths.
# Some Quartz dependencies might use underscore prefixes, and Quartz doesn't
# automatically create a .nojekyll file, so it's necessary to create it manually.
touch public/.nojekyll
 
# Last check to confirm the build output is valid; only HTML, CSS, JS, and assets
# should be published, so a stray .md file means the raw vault was synced
if find public -name '*.md' -print -quit | grep -q .; then
  echo "error: public/ contains Markdown files; aborting." >&2
  find public -name '*.md' | head >&2
  exit 1
fi
 
# --delete retires unpublished pages. These --exclude names are rsync's own
# filter syntax, not gitignore's: rsync still prunes an excluded directory
# (.git/ is never walked), but there's no upward search through parent
# .gitignore files. The CONTENT_DIR fix above depends on that upward search
# not finding a stray rule; this list is self-contained instead, so nothing
# outside this line can add a surprise exclusion here.
echo "Syncing to ${LIVE_REPO_PATH}..."
rsync -a --delete \
  --exclude='.git' --exclude='.gitignore' --exclude='README.md' \
  public/ "${LIVE_REPO_PATH}/"
 
cd "${LIVE_REPO_PATH}"
 
if [ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
  echo "No changes to publish."
  exit 0
fi
 
git add -A
git commit -m "${MESSAGE}"
git push
 
echo "Published and updated omnomnomicon.arkavian.house"
 
 

Serve
When publish.sh pushes updated main to the remote repo on GitHub, GitHub Pages serves the site directly.
Side notes and gotchas
Quartz build silently ignored the vault symlink
content/ in the staging repo is a symlink to the Obsidian vault, and it’s listed in this repo’s .gitignore because the symlink target is a different absolute path on every machine that clones this repo, so it shouldn’t be committed. However, this resulted in nothing being published when I ran publish.sh.
Why? Quartz uses globby to find content to publish, and that package traverses directories upward from the given content directory for .gitignore files. Git’s ignore behaviour treats everything nested under an ignored directory as ignored too. Which means this happens:

I pass the ignored symlink (content/) as the vault source directory to the quartz build command
Quartz finds this repo’s .gitignore, which lists content, and resulting in zero files built

The fix: resolve CONTENT_DIR to its real path with readlink -f before passing it to quartz build -d, so the ignored path is never fed to Quartz.
Bash script safety: checking variables with a leading :
Each line in the that script checks a whether a variable has been set has the : character as the first character. Bash requires an actual command on each line, so : tells Bash to evaluate the variable without running the resulting value as a command (default behaviour).
This is a much more concise way to express:
if [[ -z "${VARIABLE_NAME:-}" ]]; then
  echo "set VARIABLE_NAME" >&2
  exit 1
fi
And it’s distinct from if [[ -e $value ]], which checks whether a file actually exists at the specified path.

tech/tinkering/sewing-machine-lighting-m.title: Sewing machine lighting mod
tech/tinkering/sewing-machine-lighting-m.content:
I have a Singer 1120 sewing machine that has a built-in light too weak for the kind of sewing I need done; goths, or at least people with gothic hearts, live in this house, and a 40-watt incandescent candelabra bulb just doesn’t show black stitches on black fabric. Initially, I was thinking of an LED corncob array to use in the existing E12 socket, but the only ones I could find maxed out at 500 lumens, or 60W equivalent — hardly an improvement, considering the cost and effort.
A good friend, who plays with electronics the way I play with words, suggested instead to rewire the socket to power an LED strip along the top of the harp (a.k.a. throat). This plan was later revised to set up an LED array with its own DC power supply, leaving the existing bulb and socket alone and providing a rather terrifying amount of bright white light when needed. As he cheerfully says, “There’s no kill like overkill!”
He did almost all of the planning and assembly on this, but I tried my hand at soldering, so there’s that. I found I benefited greatly from watching someone who is very comfortable with what they do in an area I have zero practical knowledge of, since a bit of that comfort and familiarity transferred over to me and helped me feel less anxious about an area of crafting I’d previously known nothing about.
Tools and materials

White surface-mount LED panel
12-volt DC power supply
2.1 mm DC power jack with pigtail

Alternatively, if you can’t find one with wires long enough to work on your machine, get the power jack and wire separately.


Hot glue gun and hot glue
Double-sided tape
Dremel or other tool for boring a hole in plastic
Soldering iron and solder

Process


Remove the plastic housing of the sewing machine by unscrewing the case screws and gently prying the housing apart as appropriate.

You may find your owner’s manual useful here. I didn’t.


A look at how the new components are arranged and connected.

A trick to remember where the screws go: take a sheet of cardboard, draw a diagram of the machine on it, and, as you remove each screw, punch it into the corresponding place on the diagram.
If you’re like me and didn’t know the above trick until someone told you after you’d already taken the case off, then do your best not to force or cross-thread any screws when you put them back. You’ll probably find that everything works out fine.



Find an appropriate place for the power jack in the housing and drill a hole just big enough for the jack to fit snugly in.


Fit the jack into the new hole, wire side on the inside of the case, and adjust it until it’s flush with the outside of the case.


Fill any gaps between the jack and the edges of the hole with hot glue, and add more as needed to secure the jack.


Position the LED panel on the plastic case at the top of the harp, and, when satisfied with the position, mark the housing at the spot where the LED panel’s solder pads would be.


Drill a hole large enough for the power jack’s leads to pass through at the previously marked spot, then pass the leads through from the inside of the case to the outside.


Use the soldering iron to desolder the existing leads from the LED panel, then solder the power jack’s leads onto the LED panel’s pads.


Test functionality by connecting the power jack to the power supply, then to a standard wall outlet.

Do not look at the LED panel when you do this.



When satisfied with the functionality, use double-sided tape to secure the LED panel to the top of the harp, as well as to secure


Reassemble the machine and take it out for a spin!
